lead: Verilog HDL is a hardware description language. A module is the basic design block. Its port list gives the inputs and outputs; wire and reg declare connections and stored values; operators build expressions from those values. Every bit carries one of four states: 0, 1, x or z. You write this text, compile it, and simulate it before synthesis turns it into gates or FPGA logic. The same rules cover small blocks and large chips, so exam questions test reading and writing exact expressions.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for where RTL sits in the flow.

blocks.text: Verilog source is plain text. White space separates tokens; // comments to end of line and /* */ comments across lines are ignored. Identifiers start with a letter or underscore, then letters, digits, underscore or $. Identifiers are case-sensitive; keywords are lowercase. System tasks start with $, for example $display.
Number literals use size'radix value. 4'b1010 is 4 bits binary; 8'hFF is 8 bits hex; 32'd10 is 32 bits decimal. An unsized decimal like 10 is 32 bits. Strings sit in double quotes.

A module is the design block: module m (input [3:0] a, output [3:0] y); ... endmodule. The port list gives direction input, output or inout, optional type wire or reg, width such as [3:0], and name. An instance connects ports: m u1 (.a(a), .y(y));. Named connections are safer than positional order. Ports are the module's pins.

A net is a connection, not storage. wire and tri are nets. A continuous assign or a gate output drives a net. A variable holds a value between procedural assignments. reg is that variable in classic Verilog; some syllabi call reg a variable. It is assigned inside always or initial. parameter names a constant.

Vectors are ordered bits. wire [3:0] v; has v[3] as MSB and v[0] as LSB. You may select one bit v[2] or a part v[3:1]. Arrays and memories add an index after the name: reg [7:0] mem [0:15]; is 16 words of 8 bits. mem[3] is a word; mem[3][5] is one bit. wire [3:0] bus [0:7]; is an array of 8 four-bit nets.

Four-state values: 0, 1, x is unknown, z is high impedance (undriven). A reg starts as x; a wire with no driver is z. Simulation uses x for uninitialized or conflicting drivers. Synthesis must not rely on x or z as data.

Arithmetic: + - * / %. Integer division truncates toward zero; % takes the sign of the dividend. Bitwise: & | ^ ~ work bit by bit. Reduction: & | ^ ~& ~| ~^ applied to a single vector return one bit. For example, &4'b1111 is 1. Logical: && || ! return 1-bit 0 or 1; any nonzero operand is true. Relational <, <=, >, >= and equality ==, != return 1-bit 0 or 1 (x if an operand bit is x or z). Case equality === and !== also match x and z.

Shift: << is logical left shift, >> is logical right shift, and >>> is arithmetic right shift (sign-extending) for signed values. Example: 4'b0011 << 1 = 4'b0110; 4'b1000 >>> 1 = 4'b1100 for a signed operand. Conditional: cond ? a : b chooses a when cond is true. Concatenation {a,b} joins bits; replication {4{a}} repeats a. Precedence, high to low: unary and reductions, * / %, + -, shifts, relational, equality, bitwise &, ^, |, logical &&, ||, then ?: lowest.

Expression rules: an unsized decimal is 32 bits; result width is the widest operand and the assignment context. Signedness matters. x propagates through most operations. To compile and simulate at command level: iverilog -o sim design.v tb.v, then vvp sim. Commercial tools use vlog and vsim. A test bench supplies inputs; see 5.4.

spec.aria: Parse tree for the conditional expression, showing multiplication before addition, relational before conditional, and the selected true branch.

examples.question: With 4-bit unsigned values a=4, b=3, c=2, d=1, evaluate y = a + b * c > d ? (a << 1) : ~b. State y in decimal and 4-bit binary.
steps: Precedence: * before +, + before >, > before ?:. So b*c = 3*2 = 6.
10 > 1 is true, so the condition value is 1.
False branch: ~b = ~4'b0011 = 4'b1100 = 12. It is not selected.
y = 8. In four bits, 8 is written 1000.
examples.answer: y = 8 decimal; the 4-bit binary pattern is 1000.
examples.check:
a=4
b=3
c=2
d=1
bc=b*c
add=a+bc
cond=add>d
shift=a<<1
notb=(~b)&0xF
y=shift if cond else notb
print(bc)
print(add)
print(int(cond))
print(shift)
print(notb)
print(y)

traps: Bitwise ~ is not logical !. ~4'b0011 is 1100 = 12; !4'b0011 is 0 because the operand is nonzero (true).
Reduction & returns one bit; bitwise & returns a vector. &4'b1111 is 1, while 4'b1111 & 4'b1010 is 1010.
An unsized decimal literal like 10 is 32 bits. Mixing it with a 4-bit vector can widen the result; write 4'd10 when 4 bits are intended.
Conditional ?: has very low precedence. a + b > c ? x : y groups as (a + b > c) ? x : y, not as a + (b > c ? x : y).
A wire cannot store a value assigned inside an always block. Use a reg variable for procedural storage, and a wire for continuous drive.

quiz.q: What does the value z mean in a 4-state Verilog value?
quiz.a: z means high impedance, an undriven or disabled node.

quiz.q: Which keyword declares a net, and which declares a variable that holds its value between procedural assignments?
quiz.a: wire declares a net; reg declares the classic Verilog variable.

quiz.q: Why do some syllabi call reg a variable rather than a register?
quiz.a: reg holds a value between procedural assignments inside always or initial blocks. It does not always synthesize to a hardware register; the surrounding logic decides that.

quiz.q: For a=4'b1010 and b=4'b0110, compute a&b, a|b, ^a, and !a.
quiz.a: a&b = 0010. a|b = 1110. ^a = 1^0^1^0 = 0. !a = 0 because a is nonzero.

quiz.q: Evaluate y = (a + b) > 5 ? a : b for a=2, b=4.
quiz.a: a+b = 6. 6 > 5 is true, so y = a = 2.

quiz.q: A designer writes y = ~a & b with a=4'b0011, b=4'b1010. Compute y and explain the precedence.
quiz.a: ~a = 1100. 1100 & 1010 = 1000. Unary ~ binds before bitwise &, so the expression is (~a) & b.

quiz.q: Why does wire [3:0] w = 4'b1010; not behave like a reg initialized to 1010?
quiz.a: w is a net. The declaration assignment is a continuous drive, not stored state. A reg variable keeps a value between procedural assignments.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, Verilog RTL is checked by lint tools and synthesis coding guidelines before it reaches gates. SystemVerilog adds interfaces, always_ff and packed structs. Formal tools prove properties on the same modules. Search next: Verilog synthesis guidelines, SystemVerilog always_ff, lint rules, formal property checking.
